title: Epigenome Editing in Endodontics: Current Evidence and Translational Prospects
html:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Epigenome editing permits locus-specific control of gene expression without intentionally changing the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence. This critical narrative perspective assesses the small direct dental evidence base, separates molecular target engagement from tissue repair and identifies experiments needed to judge therapeutic value.

Methods

A focused narrative search examined PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception through September 17, 2026. Evidence was organised into five categories according to proximity to endodontic application. A reproducible PubMed verification search during revision identified 73 records and two unique studies eligible for the direct editing and programmable activation categories.

Results

Direct evidence is limited to locus-specific editing in human dental pulp stem cells. The FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) study demonstrated promoter acetylation in cultured cells (n = 3 for chromatin immunoprecipitation), without editor-mediated repair in vivo. The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) study reported greater dentine mineral density after transplantation of activated cells (n = 5 in the microcomputed tomography analysis; p < 0.05), although its controls could not isolate the contribution of gene activation. Broader dental studies support regulatory roles for DNA methylation, histone modification and RNA methylation. Studies outside dentistry demonstrate durable and, in selected systems, reversible epigenetic silencing in vivo. Major unresolved issues are direct pulp delivery, cell specificity, duration, off-target effects, biodistribution and long-term safety.

Conclusions

Epigenome editing could provide targeted control of reparative, regenerative and inflammatory responses in endodontics without intentional DNA sequence modification. Potential reversibility must be demonstrated for each target and editor. Current evidence supports mechanistic investigation; clinical development requires editor-attributable tissue benefit and an advantage over simpler interventions.
